citeinfo.title: August, 2022, airborne lidar survey of Mount St. Helens crater, upper North Fork Toutle River, and South Fork Toutle River

descript.abstract: The lateral blast, debris avalanche, and lahars of the May 18th, 1980, eruption of Mount St. Helens, Washington, dramatically altered the surrounding landscape. Lava domes were extruded during the subsequent eruptive periods of 1980-1986 and 2004-2008. During 2022, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contracted the acquisitions of airborne lidar surveys of Mount St. Helens crater and two primary drainages–upper North Fork Toutle River and South Fork Toutle River with GeoTerra, Inc. The U.S. Geological Survey generated a terrain dataset from the classified point cloud with supplied breaklines and modified lake hydro-flattening, then exported a single digital elevation model (DEM) of the ground surface (that is, 'bare earth'), including beneath forest cover. This USGS data release contains digital elevation and shaded relief data as 3-foot resolution raster datasets (2022dem.tif and 2022demhs.tif, respectively). This DEM can support a variety of earth science investigations.
descript.purpose: Digital elevation models are fundamental to monitoring natural hazards and studying volcanic landforms, fluvial and glacial geomorphology, and surface geology.
descript.supplinf: Lidar data acquisition, georeferencing, and classification were completed by GeoTerra, Inc. The USGS used classified points to produce a 3-foot resolution (cell size) “bare earth” DEM. Point density of “ground” classified laser returns has a high degree of spatial variation; there are areas where point density is not sufficient to support a 3-foot resolution DEM, evident by triangular-shaped artifacts resulting from interpolation (Delaunay triangulation method) between points. Values in these portions of the DEM (typically corresponding with dense vegetation and/or high topographic relief) are likely to be less accurate than areas with greater point density. Similarly, only a subset of hydrologic features have been hydroflattened, so triangular-shaped artifacts may also be present on unaltered water surfaces due to high absorption of near-infrared laser pulses. More information can be found in the supplemental data acquisition report provided.

horizpa.horizpar: A formal accuracy assessment of the horizontal positional information in the dataset has not been conducted.

vertacc.vertaccr: GeoTerra, Inc. performed a vertical accuracy assessment using GNSS static and kinematic methods. A total of 19 check points were used to determine non-vegetated (NVA) and vegetated (VVA) vertical accuracy. These check points were located in six locations; not including any on the volcano edifice or 1980 debris avalanche. Check point accuracies were reported as 0.107 feet for NVA points and 0.522 feet for VVA points (2-sigma RMSE). More details can be found in the supplemental data acquisition report provided.

procstep.procdesc: AIRCRAFT SURVEY--GeoTerra, Inc. utilized a Galaxy T2000 laser scanner, a differential GNSS system, and an inertial measurement unit mounted to a Cessna 210 aircraft to conduct airborne lidar surveys. Flight altitude was approximately 8,000 feet above ground level. GROUND SURVEY--GeoTerra conducted static GNSS surveys over known monuments. These data were used for kinematic post-processing of the aircraft GNSS data. More details can be found in the supplemental data acquisition report provided. POINT DATA PROCESSING--GeoTerra processed raw lidar data using a variety of software and techniques. Kinematic corrections for aircraft position data were resolved and smoothed best estimate of trajectory (SBET) files were developed using Inertial Explorer. Raw laser point cloud files were processed in LMS. TerraMatch and TerraScan software packages were then used for strip adjustments and automated classification. Survey control quality checks, manual cleanup, bare earth generation, and final data deliverables were completed using LP360, ArcMap, and CAD. More details can be found in the supplemental data acquisition report provided.

DEM PRODUCTION--The USGS derived a single Esri ArcGIS terrain dataset (dynamic TIN representation) from LAS and breakline files provided by GeoTerra, Inc. Hydroflattening was modified at major lakes to ensure a consistent elevation. A 3-foot resolution raster (.tif file with associated .tfw file) was then exported from the terrain dataset using linear interpolation at full resolution. Coordinate reference frame and vertical datum (NAVD88 via GEOID18) remains unchanged from the provided LAS files.
